newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria economy stabilises, growth disappoints.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria economy stabilises, growth disappoints.

text.p: Stabilisation and stagnation highlighted Nigeria's economy in 1996, with inflation dealt a severe blow but growth below target levels, a report from the central bank showed.

The annual report, obtained by Reuters on Tuesday, said that growth of 3.3 percent against a target 5.0 percent was largely accounted for by increases in production and prices of crude oil and good weather for crops.

"The realisation of the economy's full output potential continued to be constrained by inappropriate sectoral development strategies, low performing infrastructural facilities and generally inadequate level of investment," the report said.

Military-ruled Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation of more than 100 million people, has been in economic doldrums since political crisis erupted in a wave of strikes and protests after the annulment of 1993 elections.

Taking the battle against inflation as the cornerstone of tight fiscal and monetary policies, the government of General Sani Abacha scored success on that front, but has so far failed to translate relative stability into significant growth.
"The increase in aggregate output, although smaller than expected, was to a large result the extent of sustained macroeconomic stability through the year," the report said.
Inflation fell from 72.8 percent to 29.3 percent according to the figures used by the central bank.
It is estimated at 18.5 percent currently and targeted to end the year around 15 percent.
Manufacturing industry showed the first signs of improvement for several years, recording growth of 0.58 percent against a decline of 1.29 percent in 1995 and even more in previous years.

The central bank also noted a relative improvement in the health of the banking sector as a result of greater stability and decrees on failed banks and money laundering. But nonetheless said 52 of 115 licensed banks were "distressed".
Interest rates remained negative throughout the year, in spite of their deregulation in October to try and improve money market efficiency, the bank said.
"Activity in the money market was influenced largely by the high liquidity in the banking system against the background of weak demand for credit by private sector agents," the report said.

Money supply rose through 1996, but surged in the last four months of the year thanks in part to spending by the Petroleum Trust Fund, set up to cushion a 1994 fuel price rise through social spending.
The report said M2 and M1 measures of broad and narrow money supply had risen by 25.7 percent and 26.3 percent in 1996, respectively, against 10.3 percent and 8.1 percent in 1995.

The bank confirmed the government's reported budget surplus of 37 billion naira, or 1.6 percent of GDP, was in part due to a 26 billion naira windfall from higher exports of Nigeria's lifeblood crude oil.

Privately, central bank officials say the surplus was helped by using an official exchange rate of 22 naira to the dollar for some calculations and a free market rate of between 80 and 85 naira for others.

The dual exchange rate, along with effective subsidies on fuel and an apparent reluctance to privatise inefficient state enterprises is one of the sticking points Nigeria has in trying to find a way to international acceptance which could lead to help with a foreign debt of around $30 billion.
